descriptors.concept_name: Transfers Not In Good Faith To Be Void [Section 329]
descriptors.definition: Property transfers or goods deliveries made by a company within one year before a winding-up petition are void against the liquidator unless executed in the ordinary course of business or for valuable consideration in good faith. Such transactions designed to siphon off assets or evade impending liquidation proceedings are legally invalid.
inclusion: Transfers of movable or immovable property within one year before the winding up petition presentation
Delivery of goods made prior to winding up without good faith or valuable consideration
exclusion: Transfers or deliveries made in the ordinary course of business
Transfers made in favor of a purchaser or encumbrancer in good faith and for valuable consideration
nearby_distinctions: Distinct from general post-commencement transfers under Section 334, as Section 329 covers pre-petition transactions executed within one year under lack of good faith.

descriptors.definition: Any transfer or assignment executed by a company transferring all its properties or assets to trustees for the absolute benefit of all its creditors is legally void. This prevents generalized blanket conveyances outside formal insolvency resolution frameworks.
inclusion: Assignment of all company assets to trustees for creditors
exclusion: Specific property transfers for partial debt settlements not covering the entirety of assets to trustees for all creditors
nearby_distinctions: Unlike fraudulent preferences under Section 328 or bad faith transfers under Section 329, Section 330 specifically voids universal asset assignments to trustees for creditors regardless of individual transaction intent.

descriptors.concept_name: Liabilities And Rights Of Certain Persons Fraudulently Preferred [Section 331]
descriptors.definition: When a fraudulent preference involving a property-mortgaged debt is invalidated during winding up, the preferred person bears liabilities and rights as if they were a personal surety. Their liability is limited to the mortgage charge extent or the value of their interest, whichever is less.
inclusion: Determination of rights and liabilities of preferred persons as sureties
Tribunal jurisdiction to determine questions and grant relief regarding payments or transactions
exclusion: Preferences not related to property mortgaged or secured for company debt under Section 328
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from general fraudulent preference rules by establishing explicit surety-equivalent liabilities for persons holding security interests over preferred company property.

descriptors.definition: A floating charge created on a company's undertaking or property within twelve months before the commencement of winding up is invalid unless solvency immediately after creation is proved. However, it remains valid for the amount of cash paid concurrently or subsequently with interest at five percent per annum or notified rates.
inclusion: Floating charges created within 12 months preceding winding up commencement
Exceptions for contemporaneous or subsequent cash consideration with statutory interest
exclusion: Fixed charges or floating charges created earlier than 12 months prior to winding up commencement
nearby_distinctions: Differs from fixed charges by applying a strict 12-month retrospective vulnerability window and solvency proof requirement for validity during winding up.

descriptors.definition: The Company Liquidator may disclaim onerous property, burdened land, unsaleable shares, or unprofitable contracts within twelve months of winding up commencement with Tribunal leave. This disclaimer terminates the company's rights and liabilities in the property without affecting other persons' independent rights.
inclusion: Land burdened with onerous covenants
Shares or stocks in companies
Property that is unsaleable or not readily saleable
exclusion: Properties where an interested person's written request to decide on disclaimer is ignored within the statutory timeframe
nearby_distinctions: Unlike void transfers which invalidate unlawful asset disposals, disclaimer allows lawful shedding of burdensome obligations and liabilities attached to specific assets.

descriptors.concept_name: Transfers, Etc., After Commencement Of Winding Up To Be Void [Section 334]
descriptors.definition: Any disposition of a company's property, actionable claims, share transfers, or member status alterations made after the commencement of a tribunal-ordered winding up are void unless the Tribunal orders otherwise. This preserves the status quo of assets following the initiation of formal winding up proceedings.
inclusion: Property dispositions after winding up commencement
Share transfers and member status changes post-commencement
exclusion: Dispositions validated by a specific Tribunal order
nearby_distinctions: Unlike Section 329 which handles pre-petition bad faith transfers within a one-year lookback, Section 334 applies strictly to dispositions executed after the commencement of winding up.

descriptors.concept_name: Certain Attachments, Executions, Etc., In Winding Up By Tribunal To Be Void [Section 335]
descriptors.definition: Attachments, distress, executions, or property sales put in force against a company's estate without Tribunal leave after winding up commencement are void. However, this restriction exempts proceedings initiated for the recovery of government taxes, imposts, or dues.
inclusion: Attachments or executions put in force without tribunal leave post-commencement
Sales of company effects executed without tribunal leave
exclusion: Proceedings for the recovery of tax, impost, or government dues
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from general property transfers by targeting creditor-driven legal process executions, attachments, and forced sales rather than voluntary company dispositions.

descriptors.concept_name: Offences By Officers Of Companies In Liquidation [Section 336]
descriptors.definition: Officers of a company being wound up commit punishable offences if they fail to fully disclose assets, deliver property, or surrender books and papers to the liquidator. Penalized acts include concealing assets valued at one thousand rupees or more, destroying records, making false entries, or using fraud.
inclusion: Failure to disclose property and disposal details
Failure to deliver movable property and books
Concealment, destruction or falsification of books and papers
Fraudulent removal of property worth 1,000 rupees or more
exclusion: Dispositions and disclosures made in the ordinary course of business or permitted by law
nearby_distinctions: Unlike civil invalidation provisions for asset transfers, Section 336 imposes criminal liability on individual officers for active obstruction, concealment, or fraudulent non-cooperation.

descriptors.concept_name: Statement That Company Is In Liquidation [Section 344]
descriptors.definition: Every invoice, order for goods, or business letter issued by or on behalf of a company in liquidation, its liquidator, receiver, or manager must explicitly state that the company is being wound up. Contravention of this disclosure requirement attracts monetary penalties for the company, officers, and liquidator.
inclusion: Invoices issued during winding up
Goods orders and business letters bearing company name during liquidation
exclusion: Documents issued by companies not undergoing active winding up proceedings
nearby_distinctions: Differs from internal asset disclosure duties by enforcing external commercial transparency on all outward-facing transaction documents and correspondence.

descriptors.concept_name: Books And Papers Of Company To Be Evidence [Section 345]
descriptors.definition: During a company winding up, all books and papers of the company and its liquidator serve as prima facie evidence of the truth of all recorded matters as between contributories. This evidentiary status facilitates the settlement of contributories' rights and liabilities without exhaustive independent proof for every entry.
inclusion: Books and papers of the company during winding up
Records maintained by the Company Liquidator
exclusion: Conclusive evidence outside disputes strictly between contributories without rebuttal opportunity
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from standard corporate record-keeping rules by granting a statutory prima facie evidentiary presumption specifically in winding-up proceedings among contributories.

descriptors.concept_name: Inspection Of Books And Papers By Creditors And Contributories [Section 346]
descriptors.definition: Creditors and contributories may inspect a company's books and papers after a tribunal winding-up order, subject to prescribed rules. However, these restrictions do not limit inspection rights conferred by law on central or state governments, authorities, officers, or their agents.
inclusion: Inspection by creditors and contributories under prescribed rules
Unrestricted inspection rights of government authorities and officers
exclusion: Unrestricted inspection by general public members without creditor or contributory status
nearby_distinctions: Differs from general evidentiary provisions by regulating the procedural access rights of stakeholders to inspect liquidation records rather than their court admissibility.

descriptors.concept_name: Disposal Of Books And Papers Of Company [Section 347]
descriptors.definition: Upon complete winding up and prior to dissolution, a company's and liquidator's books and papers are disposed of as directed by the Tribunal. No responsibility devolves on the company, liquidator, or custodian for missing records after five years from the company's dissolution.
terminology: Company Liquidation Dividend and Undistributed Assets Account
inclusion: Disposal directions by Tribunal upon complete winding up
Immunity from record production liability after five years post-dissolution
Deposit of unpaid dividends and undistributed assets into scheduled bank accounts
exclusion: Destruction violating rules framed by the Central Government during the mandatory retention period
nearby_distinctions: Distinct from active liquidation inspection rights by governing the terminal archiving, retention limits, and ultimate destruction or deposit protocols post-dissolution.
